Enhancing Concrete Sustainability: A Critical Review of the Performance of Recycled Concrete Aggregates (RCAs) in Structural Concrete
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>In the context of sustainable construction, recycled concrete aggregates (RCAs), including both fine and coarse fractions derived from construction and demolition waste (CDW), are gaining traction due to their potential to mitigate environmental impacts by reducing reliance on natural aggregates and minimizing waste. This paper provides a comprehensive review of the effects of RCAs on the mechanical and durability properties of concrete, including compressive and tensile strengths, modulus of elasticity, and resistance to environmental degradation. The review highlights that the presence of adhered mortar and higher porosity in RCAs generally leads to reduced mechanical performance and durability. However, pretreatment methods—mechanical, chemical, and thermal—along with optimized mix designs and the use of supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs) have shown to significantly improve the concrete properties of RCAs. Additionally, recent studies on carbon dioxide (CO2) capture through the accelerated carbonation of RCAs offer promising environmental benefits. Life cycle assessment (LCA) analyses reveal reductions in energy use, CO2 emissions, and material costs when RCAs are properly processed and locally sourced. Despite challenges related to RCA quality variability, the review identifies pathways for the effective use of RCAs in structural applications.</jats:p>

crossref.title: Innovative Electrochemical Synthesis of Portland Cement Precursor (Ca(OH)2) with Machine Learning-Enabled Predictive Insights
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>For long the manufacturing of calcium hydroxide, a major precursor of cement production, has relied heavily on the calcining of calcium carbonate, which not only costs much energy, but also releases a significant amount of carbon dioxide. To electrochemically synthesize calcium hydroxide is a high-potential substitution, as it utilizes the pH gradient to decarbonate limestone and generate calcium hydroxide, which can be carried out at room temperature. But creating a pH gradient with electrolysis of water requires a relatively high voltage, which could be energy-draining in manufacturing. Hence, here an innovative three-chamber electrolysis system based on hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and hydrogen oxidation reaction (HOR) is proposed, which lowers the electrolysis voltage to ~1.7 V at 150 mA while achieving ~100% coulombic efficiency for CaCO3 dissolution. A regularized linear regression model and a multi-layer perceptron are also developed as methodological demonstrations to (i) analyze the influence of key factors, including current, electrolyte concentration, and gas flow rate, on the calcium hydroxide production rate of the system; and (ii) infer potential main constraint of the system. Ion migration behavior during electrolysis is studied, suggesting that the main constraint lies in the unwanted migration of Ca2+ and OH−. The possibility of further applying deep learning to optimize experimental parameters, recognize major restrictions from high-dimensional data, and predict test results is also discussed, with prediction reliability constrained by limited experimental samples. This work offers a conceptually promising decarbonized pathway for cement-precursor production and references for combining electrochemistry with machine learning.</jats:p>

crossref.title: Performance of recycled aggregate concrete under combined carbonation-based treatments
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>Carbonation-based treatments (CBTs) have been widely proposed to improve recycled aggregate concrete, but their combined use may not produce additive benefits. This study investigated concrete containing recycled concrete aggregates (RCA) subjected to carbonation pre-treatment, early-age carbon dioxide curing (CDC) of concrete specimens and the use of carbonated water as mixing water, applied individually and in combination. Compressive strength, dynamic modulus of elasticity, electrical resistivity and carbonation depth were evaluated under moist curing (MC), CDC and combined curing regimes, supported by qualitative microstructural observations. Under MC, concretes incorporating carbonated RCA or carbonated water achieved compressive strengths comparable with concrete made with untreated RCA. Early-age CDC alone did not markedly compromise mechanical performance, whereas combined CBTs reduced the 28-day compressive strength by about 10–20% in concretes made with carbonated RCA or carbonated water. At the same time, combined treatments increased electrical resistivity and carbonation depth. The results show that improvements in transport-related indicators do not necessarily translate into cumulative mechanical benefits when CBTs are combined.</jats:p>

crossref.abstract: <jats:p>External strengthening using fibre-reinforced polymer (FRP) is widely adopted to enhance the flexural capacity of reinforced concrete (RC) T-beams. However, brittle failure modes triggered by premature debonding remain a major challenge in structural modelling. This comparative review aims to evaluate and synthesise the agreement between finite element modelling (FEM) predictions and experimental results for RC T-beams strengthened with hybrid FRP (HFRP) and carbon FRP (CFRP) across varied strengthening configurations. A quantitative assessment was conducted on four parameters: ultimate load capacity (Pmax), critical deflections (δy, δmax, δu), displacement ductility (μΔ), and dissipated energy (Ed). The synthesis confirms that external FRP strengthening consistently increases experimental peak loads (for instance, from 236.0 kN to 291.0 kN), yet exerts opposing effects on peak deflection depending on the strengthening layout and bonded span length. The flexural capacity gains are generally accompanied by a 9-56% reduction in experimental ductility compared with control specimens, whereas transverse strip configurations preserve ductility more effectively and absorb 18-73% more energy (0.91-1.12 kJ) than full-width plates (0.65-0.77 kJ). Regarding numerical validation, FEM simulations predict ultimate load capacities with high accuracy against physical tests (such as 208.5 kN vs. 210.0 kN for BFR1 and 301.0 kN vs. 297.0 kN for SB2), but overestimate initial elastic stiffness, resulting in substantially smaller yield deflections (δy). Owing to the perfect-bond assumption that neglects post-peak brittle delamination, standard FEM analyses overestimate ductility indices (μFEM/μEksp reaching 1.12-2.32) and yield 4.13- 45.89% higher dissipated energy across most specimens. These findings underscore the necessity of incorporating cohesive zone modelling at the concrete-FRP interface to capture actual brittle failure accurately.</jats:p>

crossref.title: High-Temperature Damage Recovery of Waste Glass Cementitious Materials: Thermodynamic Prediction and Experimental Validation
crossref.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>A critical challenge for fire-resilient infrastructure lies in the inherent thermal instability of conventional cementitious composites under extreme temperatures. To address this gap, this study investigated the dosage-dependent effects of recycled glass powder (GP) in the high-temperature response of cementitious materials. Thermodynamic simulations were first used to predict GP dosage-dependent liquid-phase formation, melt viscosity, and phase assemblage evolution, and the predicted sintering window was then experimentally evaluated. The results showed that GP incorporation promoted the formation of thermally stable crystalline phases, such as rankinite, akermanite, and gehlenite, while reducing the generation of detrimental free CaO and γ-C2S. At 30% GP replacement, the paste exhibited the most favorable recovery after exposure to 1200 °C, retaining 79.3% of its initial compressive strength. After heating, moderate GP incorporation induced viscous flow assisted sintering, pore and crack closure, and ceramic-like microstructural reconstruction. In contrast, excessive GP incorporation generated an overabundant low-viscosity liquid phase, causing over-melting-related dimensional instability. Quantitatively, the residual compressive strength showed strong correlations with the content of thermally stabilized silicate phases and the liquid fraction, with R2 values of 0.939 and 0.907, respectively. These findings demonstrate that the high-temperature performance of GP-blended cement paste is governed by a dosage-dependent liquid-phase sintering, pore-network closure and phase reconstruction mechanism, providing a predictive basis for designing thermally responsive glass-cement hybrid systems.</jats:p>

crossref.title: Creep Behavior of Limestone Calcined Clay Cement Concrete under Axial Compression
crossref.container: Journal of Materials in Civil Engineering
crossref.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>To advance the practical application of limestone calcined clay cement (LC3) concrete in engineering structures, this study examines its creep behavior under axial compression for 180 days. Nineteen LC3 concrete cylinders were tested, considering different strength grades (high-performance and normal-strength LC3 concrete), calcined clay contents (20% and 30%), and stress levels (0.3–0.5 stress-to-strength ratios). Results revealed accelerated creep development during initial loading, stabilizing after two months. FRP jacketing at a low stress-to-strength ratio may only provide a sealed condition for concrete core rather than confinements. The estimated drying creep strains approximately accounted for 20% of the total creep strains. Normal-strength LC3 specimens demonstrated 20–30% greater creep coefficients than high-performance LC3 concrete counterparts, attributable to its higher water-to-binder ratio, porous interfacial transition zones, and differences in hydration products. Microstructural analysis showed that 30% calcined clay content in high-performance LC3 concrete produced a less dense C-(A)-S-H matrix with floc-like morphology compared to the 20% mixture, explaining its 12% higher creep. The nonlinear creep threshold exceeded 0.5 for high-performance LC3 concrete with 30% calcined clay, though this limit may vary with different replacement ratios. Whereas existing ultra-high performance concrete models could predict creep in high-performance LC3 concrete with reasonable errors, applications of existing creep models to normal-strength LC3 concrete required substantial modifications. These findings provide critical insights for implementing LC3 concrete in structural applications while highlighting the importance of LC3 composition-dependent creep characteristics.</jats:p>

crossref.abstract: <jats:p>How does a mortar change when biochar absorbs part of its mixing water, or when treated effluent replaces drinking water? The authors trace rice-husk, rice-straw and sewage-sludge biochars from their production to their use in ordinary Portland cement (OPC) and limestone calcined clay cement (LC³). They draw on six studies from Pakistan. Four have published reports, and the authors report the results of the other two in the book. The chapters follow the mixtures from the fresh state through strength development, water absorption and durability. They also compare wastewater sources used in concrete pavers and examine a mortar made with both treated effluent and biochar from sewage sludge. For researchers, graduate students and practising engineers, the final chapter and a worked example show how to compare mixtures when their advantages differ. A mix that saves potable water or lowers calculated carbon emissions may also absorb more water. The ranking depends on which properties matter for the intended use.</jats:p>

crossref.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Three-dimensional concrete printing (3DCP) is emerging as a sustainable technology because of automation and material efficiency. However, high Portland cement content compromises its environmental impact. Although using supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs) is a promising pathway to improve the environmental sustainability of printable mixtures, their technical and environmental viability is still a challenge. A systematic literature review was performed to understand the feasibility of standard and alternative SCMs as partial Portland cement replacements in 3DCP by considering technical feasibility, legal barriers, fresh state behaviour, and hardened performance. Standard SCMs have well-established standards and treatment processes, but their local availability and supply issues limit their use. Although SCMs from alternative sources, such as waste and by-products, can enhance resource efficiency and sustainability, their feasibility is limited by physical and chemical properties, which impact fresh and hardened performance. Thus, ground granulated blast furnace slag, fly ash, limestone powder, ornamental stone waste, and waste glass powder improve flowability, pumpability, and extrudability, while silica fume, calcined clay, metakaolin, burnt oil shale, construction and demolition waste powders, waste brick powder, and municipal solid waste are generally responsible for increasing the buildability and shape retention. Hence, ternary binders with Portland cement and two SCMs are commonly used to optimise fresh properties and achieve the desirable printability and hardened performance. The literature review indicates that combining SCMs with complementary rheological effects allows for achieving a balance between flowability and shape retention during the printing process. However, future life cycle assessments of printable mixtures with sensitivity analyses, including transport distance, treatment, and valorisation strategies, are required to boost the incorporation of alternative SCMs in printable mixtures.</jats:p>

crossref.title: Data-Driven Optimization of Calcined Kaolin Waste for Sustainable Alkali-Activated Binders
crossref.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Kaolin beneficiation generates large volumes of fine mineral residues with limited direct industrial application, despite their high aluminosilicate content and potential as reactive precursors. This study investigates the structural transformation of an industrial kaolin waste through thermal activation and its subsequent conversion into a hybrid alkali-activated binder. X-ray diffraction, FTIR, and SEM revealed the progressive collapse of the crystalline kaolinite lattice and the development of a predominantly amorphous aluminosilicate structure after calcination at 750 °C for 4 h. Thermogravimetric analysis of the optimized binder further revealed its thermal behavior up to 900 °C, supporting the formation of alkali-activated binding phases. To address the strong nonlinear coupling among precursor ratio, activator chemistry, and water content, a design of experiments and machine learning framework was applied to 41 metakaolin waste−slag formulations. Gaussian Process Regression outperformed ensemble tree-based models (R2 = 0.962 vs. ≤0.783) and provided predictive uncertainty maps that guided the search toward formulation regions combining high predicted strength with low predictive uncertainty. The identified optimum was experimentally validated, achieving 28.5 ± 0.9 MPa after 7 days of curing at 70 °C, with a prediction error of 1.35%. The optimized binder was further investigated by XRD, FTIR, SEM/EDS, and thermogravimetric analysis. Overall, the results demonstrate an uncertainty-aware, data-driven strategy for optimizing waste-derived alkali-activated binders and provide a transferable framework for materials design based on underutilized mineral residues.</jats:p>

crossref.abstract: <jats:p>The cement industry faces increasing pressure to reduce clinker consumption and utilize industrial by-products more efficiently. This study investigated the mechanical, internal-quality, and waste-utilization performance of Portland Composite Cement (PCC) mortar incorporating Class F fly ash (FA). Five mixtures containing 0%, 10%, 20%, 30%, and 40% FA as a mass replacement for PCC were prepared. The water-to-binder ratio was adjusted from 0.534 to 0.620 to maintain a constant flow of 190 mm. Cubic specimens measuring 50 × 50 × 50 mm were tested at 7, 28, and 90 days using the point load test and ultrasonic pulse velocity (UPV). One-way ANOVA and Tukey’s HSD test were applied to the 28-day results, while Waste Diversion Rate (WDR) and Waste Mechanical Performance Index (WMPI) were used to assess waste-utilization efficiency. Point load strength and UPV increased with curing age for all mixtures. At 90 days, the 10% FA mixture achieved the highest point load strength and UPV, reaching 1.150 MPa and 3732.1 m/s, respectively, exceeding the control values of 1.011 MPa and 3419.2 m/s. At 28 days, FA replacement significantly affected point load strength and UPV, with p-values of 0.016 and 0.006, respectively. Tukey’s HSD showed that mixtures containing up to 30% FA remained statistically comparable to the control, whereas 40% FA caused significant reductions. WDR and WMPI increased continuously with FA content, reaching 9.11% and 0.0829 at 40% replacement. Overall, 10% FA provided the best long-term performance, while 30% FA offered the most balanced combination of engineering performance and waste utilization.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The utilisation of waste wood in cement-bonded composites addresses pressing ecological challenges by diverting municipal waste wood from incineration. In this study, a life cycle assessment (LCA) was conducted on a pilot-sized wood-cement composite board (1 × 1 m²; 18 mm thick) incorporating 25 wt% waste wood converted into wood chips. Environmental impacts were quantified for standard categories, including global warming, acidification, eutrophication, etc., in accordance with ISO 14044 guidelines. The results showed that Ordinary Portland cement was the dominant contributor to all impact categories, whereas the waste wood had negligible cradle burden. The composite product achieved a global warming potential of approx. 10.7 kg CO₂-eq., substantially lower than comparable cement-based composite boards on the market (14–32 kg CO₂-eq.). Primary energy demand of the boards was 40–70% less than that of commercial alternatives, benefiting from the use of bio-based waste and a cleaner energy mix in production. The composite boards exhibited a favourable environmental profile while maintaining acceptable mechanical performance for non-structural applications, thus providing a sustainable outlet for municipal waste wood. The findings support the viability of upcycling municipal waste wood into value-added building materials in line with circular economy goals.</jats:p>

crossref.title: Optimization of Fonio Husk Ash and Calcined Waste Treatment Sludge for Age-Dependent Compressive Strength of Portland Limestone Cement Concrete
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>The sustainable application of agro-industrial and treatment facility waste-based materials in concrete requires the collective assessment of material reactivity, substitution amount and strength development. This study examined the combined effects of fonio husk ash (FHA), calcined waste-treatment sludge (CWTS) and curing age on the compressive strength of Portland limestone cement (PLC) concrete via a face-centered central composite design (FCCD) with response surface methodology (RSM). Physicochemical characterization revealed high surface areas for FHA and CWTS, whereas X-ray fluorescence analysis revealed combined SiO2 + Al2O3 + Fe2O3 contents of 82.24% and 73.20%, respectively. The compressive strength was evaluated at 7, 28, 56 and 90 days. The strength increased with increasing curing age, whereas excessive combined replacement reduced the strength, indicating that clinker loss becomes dominant beyond a threshold. The RSM models demonstrated strong predictive ability, with R2 values ranging from 0.9969 to 0.9998. Numerical optimization produced optimal FHA and CWTS contents of 7.63% and 10.21%, respectively, at a desirability of 0.728. The validation results revealed errors of less than 4% across all curing ages. Thus, FCCD-RSM reliably captured composition- and age-dependent strength trends, providing a basis for valorizing agro-industrial and treatment wastes in lower-clinker PLC concrete.</jats:p>

crossref.abstract: <jats:p>In the Moroccan cement industry, searching for alternatives to clinker using noncalcined mineral additions has become a significant focus to reduce energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions and produce cement with a low environmental impact. This study examines the effects of incorporating Triassic basalts and Liassic limestone on the mechanical properties of mortars, as well as cement color, water demand, setting time, and durability of cement – based composites. The pozzolanic activity of basalt, calculated from chemical composition and amorphous phase content, is proposed as an intrinsic index of pozzolanic activity. The pozzolanic activity strength index was evaluated as the ratio of the compressive strength of the blended basalt – limenstone/cement mortar to that of a control Portland cement. Mortars with 10–15% of El Hajeb basalt and 19–24% limestone exhibited optimal mechanical performance at early (2 d) and long-term (28 d) stages, while improving setting times. Additionally, these combinations offer improved environmental and economic benefits for the production of pozzolanic CEMIV and CEMII composite cements, which comply with international standards (ASTM C618, 2022; EN 197-5, 2021; and NM 10, 01, 004, 2019).</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Calcium carbonate is widely used as a low‐carbon component in cementitious binders, but its effect is commonly discussed in terms of dilution, filler effects and nucleation. The potential influence of CaCO
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    polymorphs remains less understood. This study compares calcite‐dominant limestone powder (LSP) and aragonite‐rich mussel shell powder (MSP) as partial replacements for Portland cement. Cement pastes containing 5–20 wt.% LSP or MSP were prepared to investigate the effects of CaCO
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    polymorphs on hydration kinetics, phase assemblage, mechanical performance and microstructure. Both carbonate powders accelerated early hydration by providing additional nucleation sites. Compared with LSP, MSP showed a stronger hydration‐promoting effect at moderate replacement levels, which is attributed to the metastable aragonite structure and its enhanced interaction with aluminate phases. The use of MSP promoted the formation of C–S–H and carbonate‐bearing AFm phases, leading to comparable or improved early strength at replacement levels not exceeding 10 wt.%. At 20 wt.% replacement, dilution became more pronounced and showed limited strength development. These results indicate that mussel shell powder can be regarded as a waste‐derived substitute from marine of limestone, which is a carbonate source with polymorph‐dependent reactivity for low‐carbon cement pastes.
                  </jats:p>

crossref.abstract: <jats:p>Cracking continues to be the number one concern about bridge deck construction. Rarely is a deck without cracks constructed. Transverse cracking mainly attributable to drying shrinkage is common in bridge decks and has been observed in many bridge decks newly constructed by the Virginia Department of Transportation (DOT). Shrinkage-reducing admixtures (SRAs) in concrete reduce shrinkage and are one of the most effective ways of reducing shrinkage cracking. A low modulus of elasticity and high creep also help minimize cracking. Lightweight concrete (LWC) has a lower modulus of elasticity, higher inelastic strains, a lower coefficient of thermal expansion, a more continuous contact zone between the aggregate and the paste, and more water in the pores of aggregates for continued internal curing than normal weight concrete: all these factors help reduce cracking in LWC. Drying shrinkage can also be counteracted with the use of shrinkage-compensating concrete (SC). When properly restrained by reinforcement, SC can expand an amount equal to or slightly greater than the anticipated drying shrinkage. The research in this paper investigated the effectiveness of SC, LWC, and concrete with SRA in reducing cracks in bridge decks and to develop a low-cracking bridge deck specification for use in future Virginia DOT bridge decks. The study showed that bridges with fewer and narrower cracks could be constructed with SRA, LWC, and SC and that proper construction practices were needed to reduce bridge deck cracking. This study resulted in the Virginia DOT implementing a low-cracking bridge deck specification.</jats:p>

crossref.abstract: <jats:p>Release of carbon dioxide (CO<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>) from fossil fuel combustion and cement manufacture is the primary anthropogenic driver of climate change. Our best estimate is that China became the largest national source of CO<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> emissions during 2006. Previously, the United States (US) had occupied that position. However, the annual emission rate in the US has remained relatively stable between 2001–2006 while the emission rate in China has more than doubled, apparently eclipsing that of the US in late 2006. Here we present the seasonal and spatial pattern of CO<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> emissions in China, as well as the sectoral breakdown of emissions. Though our best point estimate places China in the lead position in terms of CO<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> emissions, we qualify this statement in a discussion of the uncertainty in the underlying data (3–5% for the US; 15–20% for China). Finally, we comment briefly on the implications of China's new position with respect to international agreements to mitigate climate change.</jats:p>

crossref.abstract: <jats:p>In this study, optimization of durability properties of the concretes was performed by using Taguchi method and Anova analysis. The durability performance of the concretes was evaluated using measurements of rapid chloride ion permeability, freezing-thawing resistance and sorptivity tests. The degree of freezing-thawing resistance was assessed the change of weight, ultrasonic pulse velocity (UPV) and flexural strength after 300 cycles. The use of fly ash improved the rapid chloride ion permeability and sorptivity of concrete. The best resistance to chloride ion permeability was obtained from a combination of type of class C fly ash content of 102 kg/m3 with PC content of 332 kg/m3. There was a remarkable reduction in the UPV after the specimens are subjected to freezing-thawing cycles. The amounts of flexural strength loss have been measured in the range of 6.70 - 29.83%. The use of type of class C fly ash positively affected freezing-thawing resistance of concrete. The Anova analysis indicated that the cement dosage has an utmost importance on the sorptivity level, chloride ion permeability and ultrasonic pulse velocity loss. Furthermore, the fly ash percentage has an utmost importance on the weight loss and flexural strength loss.</jats:p>

crossref.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="fr">La valorisation des sédiments marins du GPMD comme un nouveau granulat présente une solution alternative dans le domaine de génie civil. Les travaux de cette thèse se focalisent sur l’étude de valorisation du sédiment en technique routière et l’étude de durabilité du béton à base de sédiment. La première partie de la thèse fait l’objet de la valorisation des sédiments marins en technique routière. Elle est devisée en trois étapes :La première étape a été consacrée à une identification du sédiment marin. La deuxième étape présente la méthodologie de valorisation du sédiment par la mise au point d’une formulation en laboratoire. La dernière étape concerne la réalisation d’un ouvrage routier à l’échelle 1 à base du sédiment à Dunkerque. La phase de suivi in situ de l’aspect mécanique et environnemental de l’ouvrage est également traitée. La seconde partie fait l’objet d’une étude de durabilité du béton à base de sédiment. Cette partie est divisée en trois étapes. La première étape est consacrée à une caractérisation non destructive et destructive des deux bétons contenant 12,5% et 20% de sédiment associé à une caractérisation microstructurale. La deuxième concerne l’étude de durabilité du béton face à l’attaque sulfatique externe, aux cycles gel/dégel et à la RAG afin d’évaluer l’effet de l’ajout de sédiment dans le béton. Enfin, la troisième étape traite l’impact environnemental sur les deux types de bétons. L’étude de durabilité des bétons à base de sédiment présentée dans cette partie peut servir de base à des futurs travaux visant à mieux comprendre l’impact d’incorporation de sédiment dans le béton sur la résistance mécanique, ainsi que sur les mécanismes de dégradation.</jats:p>

crossref.abstract: <jats:p>Resumo Os resíduos incorporados aos materiais de construção devem ser usados, se possível, sem processamentos, para evitar o aumento dos impactos ambientais e custos adicionais. A cinza de casca de arroz (CCA) é uma pozolana que deve ser previamente moída, para aumentar a finura e a reatividade com o cimento, quando empregada como material cimentício. Este trabalho estuda cinza de casca de arroz natural (CCAN) sem processamento em substituição parcial de 15% de cimento, em massa, para uso em concreto estrutural, cominuída por moagem conjunta com os agregados no tambor da betoneira. Na parte I desta pesquisa, já publicada, são apresentados os resultados de microestrutura, resistência mecânica e retração, também para o teor de 25%, e nesta parte II são mostrados os dados dos ensaios de durabilidade (carbonatação, penetração de cloretos, resistividade, absorção d'água, permeabilidade ao oxigênio, absorção capilar e reação álcali-sílica - RAS), comparados ao concreto referência com 100% de cimento e, ainda, com CCA moída previamente (CCAM). Os resultados mostram que 15% de CCAN é factível de ser empregado em concreto porque apresenta desempenho superior ao concreto referência, quando usado cimento com pozolanas e próximos ou até superiores às misturas de CCAM, para grande parte das variáveis estudadas. Conclui-se que 15% de CCAN para concreto estrutural é viável e traz maior sustentabilidade.</jats:p>

crossref.title: Concretos com cinza do bagaço da cana-de-açúcar: avaliação da durabilidade por meio de ensaios de carbonatação e abrasão
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>O bagaço é gerado como resíduo do processamento do açúcar e do álcool. Esse resíduo é utilizado para a cogeração de energia por meio da queima em caldeiras, restando ao final as cinzas residuais do bagaço da cana-de-açúcar (CBC). Atualmente, essas cinzas são aproveitadas nas lavouras de cana como adubação orgânica, apesar de ser um material com poucos nutrientes. O objetivo deste trabalho foi avaliar a durabilidade de concretos que utilizaram a CBC em substituição ao agregado miúdo por meio de ensaios de carbonatação e abrasão. Os resultados foram comparados aos obtidos para um concreto sem CBC. Os concretos foram dosados para que tivessem a mesma consistência e o mesmo teor de argamassa. Produziram-se traços com 0%, 30% e 50% de CBC, em substituição ao agregado miúdo em três grupos diferentes. Foram realizados ensaios mecânicos e, a partir dos resultados obtidos, os concretos que apresentaram os melhores resultados foram submetidos ao ensaio de carbonatação, nas idades de 60, 120 e 210 dias, e ao ensaio de abrasão superficial, aos 28 dias. Os resultados obtidos permitiram concluir que a carbonatação e a abrasão do concreto produzido com a CBC como substituto parcial do agregado miúdo e o cimento CP II E 32 são similares ao concreto sem adição da cinza.</jats:p>

crossref.title: A importância da segregação do agregado reciclado na resistência e na durabilidade do concreto estrutural
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>Resumo A heterogeneidade dos resíduos de construção e demolição dificulta seu uso sistemático, consequentemente, têm-se problemas com a disposição final e a contínua extração e uso de recursos não renováveis para fabricação de concretos. Essa heterogeneidade decorre, majoritariamente, da não segregação dos diversos constituintes dos resíduos durante seu processamento. O presente artigo analisa a necessidade da segregação dos resíduos de construção e demolição em diferentes tipos - cerâmicas de argila e cimentícios - e as consequências da utilização desses materiais como substituintes dos agregados naturais graúdos em concretos estruturais. Para tanto, foram fabricados concretos com 0, 25, 50 e 100% de agregados reciclados, sendo três tipos de resíduos utilizados: cimentícios, cerâmicos e uma mistura dos dois, nas proporções obtidas na usina de reciclagem. As conclusões apontam não ser necessária a segregação do resíduo utilizado, uma vez que os resultados apresentam desempenho similar dos concretos com agregados cimentícios e com agregados mistos. As performances reológica e mecânica são parâmetros afetados negativamente pela adição de resíduos. Já o desempenho com relação à durabilidade pode ser melhorado com o uso de agregados reciclados.</jats:p>

crossref.abstract: <jats:p>This report presents the results of a survey of sulfate resistance tests (ASTM C452 and ASTM C1012) conducted by PCA members on portland cements and portland-limestone cements produced at 32 cement plants in North America. The survey responses are analyzed in combination with additional test data provided for cements produced at five non-PCA-member cement plants, and published data from 2019 on Type V cements from ten cement plants. There is a correlation between ASTM C1012 results and ASTM C452 results for ASTM C595 Type IL cements similar to the correlation between ASTM C1012 and ASTM C452 results for ASTM C150 Type II and V cements. Type IL cements currently meeting 6-month ASTM C1012 expansion limits for sulfate resistant designations in ASTM C595 generally would also meet 14-day ASTM C452 expansion limits currently in CSA A3001, although there are some differences between the tests with respect to designating cements as high sulfate resistant or moderate sulfate resistant. Revisions to ASTM and AASHTO standard specifications for sulfate resistance designations for Type IL (portland-limestone) cements are recommended to permit these designations based upon 14-day expansion results in the ASTM C452 mortar bar test, while also retaining the option to base designations upon ASTM C1012 test results.</jats:p>

crossref.title: Roadmap for Decarbonization of the Building and Construction Industry—A Supply Chain Analysis Including Primary Production of Steel and Cement
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>Sweden has committed to reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions to net-zero by 2045. Around 20% of Sweden’s annual CO2 emissions arise from manufacturing, transporting, and processing of construction materials for construction and refurbishment of buildings and infrastructure. In this study, material and energy flows for building and transport infrastructure construction is outlined, together with a roadmap detailing how the flows change depending on different technical and strategical choices. By matching short-term and long-term goals with specific technology solutions, these pathways make it possible to identify key decision points and potential synergies, competing goals, and lock-in effects. The results show that it is possible to reduce CO2 emissions associated with construction of buildings and transport infrastructure by 50% to 2030 applying already available measures, and reach close to zero emissions by 2045, while indicating that strategic choices with respect to process technologies and energy carriers may have different implications on energy use and CO2 emissions over time. The results also illustrate the importance of intensifying efforts to identify and manage both soft and hard barriers and the importance of simultaneously acting now by implementing available measures (e.g., material efficiency and material/fuel substitution measures), while actively planning for long-term measures (low-CO2 steel or cement).</jats:p>
